description: A pure CALCULATION node — matrices in, a whole PLAN DOCUMENT out. The inverse of Graph Interpreter: takes a typed edge list from a Math Engine and writes the standard plan JSON, objects and their parameters attached, ready to import. Draws nothing on canvas.
instructions:
THE WRITE HALF OF THE CODEC. Graph Interpreter reads the canvas into matrices; this writes matrices back out as a plan. Between them a flow can read a drawing, compute over it and emit a new one without ever materialising anything.

It is NOT Points to Graph. That node emits a GRAPH — nodes, edges, thickness, type — which still needs a Network node to become canvas segments, and a graph has nowhere to carry an attachment. This emits the full document: `schemaVersion`, `settings`, `nodes`, `segments`, `spaces`, `layers`, with each segment carrying its parametric object, that object's PARAMS and its library PATH. The result is the same shape the canvas exports, so it imports straight back.

INPUTS — one row per edge, all row-aligned, all in anchor-relative METRES (the frame every value output speaks):
• a / b — edge start and end points (N x 2)
• thickness — per edge (N x 1); falls back to the type's own thickness where 0
• types — an integer CODE per edge, 1-based into `typeNames`
• spaces — OPTIONAL space boundaries as one flat [x, y, groupIndex] matrix. Leave it unwired and the canvas derives rooms from the wall loops on import, which is usually what you want: a space references NODE IDS, so its corners have to coincide with real segment endpoints to be worth writing.

NODES ARE DEDUPLICATED BY POSITION, so a junction where four walls meet becomes ONE node with four segments on it rather than eight loose endpoints — the same rule the canvas's own exporter follows. Points are compared after rounding to `decimals`, because two endpoints a ten-thousandth of a millimetre apart are the same junction and would otherwise write two nodes that never join.

`typeMap` is where the parametric objects live: a JSON object keyed by type name, each entry naming the `segmentType` the canvas should use, the `layer`, and the object to attach — `objectId`, `objectPath` (the library link) and `params`. Anything omitted is simply left off that segment. An `opening: true` entry marks the segment as a door/window gap.

COORDINATES GO OUT IN PIXELS, metres x `pixelsPerMeter`, because that is what a plan document stores; `settings.pixelsPerMeter` is written alongside so the reader can convert back.

NODE-HOSTED OBJECTS — furniture and anything else that sits at a POINT rather than along a segment. Wire `points` (N x 2 metres), `pointTypes` (the code column) and optionally `pointRotation`, and name the objects in `pointTypeMap`. Each point becomes a node carrying its object.

Each one also gets a DEGENERATE MARKER SEGMENT, from that node back to itself, and it is not decoration: the plan reader rebuilds node metadata under a key derived from the segment ends meeting at the node, so a node no segment touches has no key and its attachments are silently DROPPED on import. The marker is what gives the node a key. It is the same thing the canvas's own exporter writes for a node-hosted object.

ONE MAP, NOT FIVE. `objects` holds `segments`, `points` and `space`. A code column indexes its map by KEY ORDER — JSON preserves insertion order, so the map's own ordering is the code table and no parallel array of names is needed. Params are OVERRIDES only: the editor fills every parameter from the object's own defaults before applying an attachment's, so an entry needs to name only what differs.

parameters.label: Objects (JSON)
parameters.help: Everything the plan attaches, in one map. `segments` keyed by edge-type name in CODE ORDER, `points` keyed by object-type name in code order, `space` the object every space carries. Each entry names its objectId, its objectPath and any params that differ from the object's own defaults.
